title: From Gas to Stone: How Scientists Are Turning Carbon Dioxide Into Rock
excerpt: Researchers in Iceland, MIT, and South Korea are advancing carbon mineralization technologies that convert CO2 into solid minerals, offering permanent climate storage solutions.
body:
• Multiple research teams — including MIT, KAIST, and Iceland's CarbFix project — are advancing technologies that convert CO2 into solid minerals, locking it away permanently as stone
  • In Iceland, the CarbFix project has demonstrated that 95% of injected CO2 can mineralize within two years when pumped into underground basalt formations
  • MIT researchers used X-ray imaging to show that mineral formation quickly reduces rock permeability but does not halt the carbon storage process
  • KAIST and MIT scientists have also developed a seawater-based approach that extracts dissolved CO2 and converts it into carbonate minerals while producing hydrogen as a byproduct

Turning Emissions Into Rock

Scientists are making rapid progress on a deceptively simple idea: turning carbon dioxide into stone. Across multiple research programs — from the volcanic fields of Iceland to laboratories in Massachusetts and South Korea — teams are refining technologies that convert the greenhouse gas into solid minerals, offering what may be the most permanent form of carbon storage available.

The concept, known as carbon mineralization, accelerates a natural geological process. When CO2-rich fluid flows through certain rocks, chemical reactions convert the carbon into carbonate minerals such as calcite or dolomite. In nature, this takes thousands of years. Researchers are compressing that timeline to months.

Iceland's CarbFix: The Proof of Concept

The most advanced demonstration is Iceland's CarbFix project, which injects CO2-rich water into underground basalt formations near Reykjavik. The project has shown that more than 95% of injected carbon dioxide turns into solid minerals within just two years — a geological flash.

Basalt, a volcanic rock that makes up roughly 70% of Earth's surface, is rich in iron, calcium, and magnesium. When these elements react with CO2 dissolved in water, they form carbonate minerals that effectively lock the carbon underground permanently.

Building on CarbFix's success, Swiss company Climeworks operates two direct air capture facilities in Iceland — Orca and the larger Mammoth plant — that suck CO2 directly from the atmosphere and inject it underground for mineralization. Together, the facilities aim to remove 40,000 tonnes of CO2 annually, though costs remain high at roughly $1,000 per tonne.

MIT's X-Ray Breakthrough

A study from MIT published in AGU Advances offers new insights into what happens inside the rock during mineralization. Researchers injected fluids into Icelandic basalt samples and used X-ray CT scanning to watch mineral formation reshape the rock's internal structure over weeks.

The experiments revealed that minerals initially form in tiny microcracks connecting larger pore spaces, quickly reducing permeability. But critically, the process does not stall.

"If you were injecting CO2 into the Earth and saw a massive drop in permeability, some operators might think they clogged up the well. But as this study shows, in some cases, it might not matter that much."

— Jonathan Simpson, MIT researcher

The findings could help engineers design more efficient underground carbon storage systems by predicting how reservoir rocks will behave over time.

From Seawater to Stone

Meanwhile, researchers at KAIST in South Korea and MIT have developed a parallel approach that targets carbon dissolved in seawater. The ocean absorbs roughly a quarter of human CO2 emissions, and the new technology uses an electrochemical process to extract that dissolved carbon and convert it into stable mineral deposits.

The method produces carbonate minerals such as calcium carbonate and magnesium hydroxide — materials with potential applications in construction and manufacturing — while also generating hydrogen gas as a byproduct. Researchers say the approach could be particularly valuable in coastal regions without access to volcanic basalt.

Scaling the Challenge

Despite the technical progress, scaling carbon mineralization to climate-relevant volumes remains a formidable challenge. Scientists estimate that billions of metric tons of CO2 must be captured and stored by the end of the century to avoid the worst impacts of climate change.

In Texas, Occidental Petroleum is building a direct air capture plant designed to remove 500,000 tonnes of CO2 annually. King Abdullah University of Science and Technology in Saudi Arabia has demonstrated a water-recycling system for CO2 mineralization in arid environments, removing one of the main barriers to deploying the technology outside Iceland's water-rich geology.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has said that without carbon capture and storage, limiting global warming to 2°C may not be possible.
